title: Not Ruling by Fear
note: Not doing what frightens the people, what frightens his officers, or what leaves the ruler himself afraid. Such acts belong with the crooked sceptre, so this chapter follows it.

couplets.plain: A ruler is one who looks into a wrong fairly and punishes to fit it, so that it won’t be done again.
couplets.pm: When a man goes against someone weaker, the true ruler looks into it impartially and, so that he won’t do it again, punishes him in measure with the offence. It follows that failing to examine fairly, and punishing too much for some other reason, are acts that frighten subjects.

links.quote: punishes to fit it
A ruler is one who looks into a wrong fairly
so that it won’t be done again

couplets.plain: Raise the blow sharply but let it land softly, if you want your gains to stay with you for long.
couplets.pm: Those who want prosperity to stay long with them should begin a punishment as if to go beyond the measure, but keep within it when they carry it out. Raising it sharply makes wrongdoers afraid, and striking softly keeps everyone else from dread. Raising and striking are images.

links.quote: Raise the blow sharply but let it land softly
links.reason: Lasting gains come from raising the blow sharply and letting it land softly.

links.remove: The rod is the old English’s. The Tamil says only raise and strike, and he calls those images.

couplets.plain: A wielder of the cruel sceptre, who lives by what terrifies people, is sure to fall, and soon.
couplets.pm: If a ruler lives by acts that terrify his subjects and is cruel in his sceptre, he is certain to fall quickly. Those acts and that ruin are told in what follows.

links.quote: lives by what terrifies people
links.reason: Rule by terror is sure to bring a ruler down, and soon.

links.quote: A wielder of the cruel sceptre
the cruel sceptre
links.reason: The cruel sceptre pictures a rule that only hurts.

couplets.plain: A ruler of whom people say the bitter words “Our ruler is harsh” will see his days shortened and soon fall.
couplets.pm: A ruler of whom his subjects speak the bitter words “our ruler is harsh” has his life cut short and quickly loses his wealth. The words are bitter because they come from hurt hearts and bring harm. His span becomes shorter than that of rulers not spoken of this way.

links.quote: Our ruler is harsh
A ruler of whom people say the bitter words

couplets.plain: The great wealth of someone hard to see, with a sour face, is like something a demon has laid eyes on.
couplets.pm: The great wealth of a man whom those who want to see him can rarely see, and whose face is unpleasant when they do, has the fault of something a demon has seized. No one goes near him, so his wealth is of no use to him or to anyone else. Seeing here means taking possession.

links.quote: someone hard to see
links.reason: One who is hard to see holds riches as useless as something a demon has seized.

links.quote: a sour face

links.remove: The Tamil names no ruler, only someone with a sour face.

couplets.plain: If you have a harsh tongue and no kind eye, even vast wealth will perish at once, without lasting.
couplets.pm: If a ruler has harsh speech and no kindly regard, his great wealth doesn’t last but perishes then and there. Harsh speech and excessive punishment, two of the seven vices, are counted here among the acts that frighten. “Great” shows that wealth is not so small that these should end it at once, and yet they do.

links.quote: a harsh tongue
no kind eye
links.reason: Having no kind eye for others hastens the end of all one has.

links.remove: The Tamil names no ruler. He supplies one, and the old English follows him.

couplets.plain: Harsh words and punishment past all measure are the file that wears away a ruler’s conquering strength.
couplets.pm: Harsh words and punishment beyond the offence are files that wear down the iron of a ruler’s strength to beat his enemies. Harsh words ruin his army, excessive punishment ruins his land, and so his strength shrinks. He calls that strength iron to show that even hard things wear away. The ruler who does these loses life, strength and wealth.

links.quote: punishment past all measure
the file that wears away a ruler’s conquering strength
links.reason: Harshness is the file that wears a ruler’s strength thin.

links.quote: Harsh words and punishment past all measure

couplets.plain: If a ruler who doesn’t think things through with his circle flies into a rage, his good fortune shrinks.
couplets.pm: A ruler who doesn’t share the thinking with his ministers and work it through with them, and who rages at them when the work fails, sees his wealth shrink daily. Ministers are his circle because they share his burden. If he blames them and rages, they take fright and leave, and then he has no way to set it right or to carry the burden.

links.quote: flies into a rage
doesn’t think things through with his circle
a ruler who doesn’t think things through

couplets.plain: A ruler who doesn’t build defences before war comes will take fright when it does, and quickly fall.
couplets.pm: A ruler who doesn’t build a fort as his refuge before war comes takes fright when it comes, having no safety, and falls quickly. Those with him fear the enemy and leave, so he is alone and afraid, and he falls into the enemy’s power.

links.quote: doesn’t build defences before war comes
A ruler who doesn’t build defences
links.reason: Warns the ruler who has built no defences when war comes.

couplets.plain: A harsh sceptre binds the unlearned to itself. The earth has no burden but that.
couplets.pm: A ruler of the harsh sceptre gathers round him as officers men unlearned in statecraft and other books. The earth has no extra burden but that gathering. He gathers only those who will do such work with him. The earth bears everything else by nature, so this alone is a burden to it.

links.quote: A harsh sceptre binds the unlearned to itself
links.reason: Calls harsh rule that binds the unlearned to itself the one true weight on the earth.

links.quote: The earth has no burden but that
links.reason: Pictures the earth as bearing no burden but this one.
